sections.title: High-Level Cause and Effect Analysis
sections.content: At Level 3, the relationship between cause and effect is not always obvious. Sometimes there is a long time gap between events, multiple global factors may influence outcomes, or the result may be part of a complex reaction system. Therefore, simply observing the sequence of events is not enough; we must deeply understand the logical structure, timing, and impact framework.

sections.title: Time Lagged Causation
sections.content: Sometimes the effect of a policy or decision does not appear immediately but becomes visible after several years. For example, if a country implements a new geopolitical trade policy and global trade balance shifts years later, there might be a causal connection. However, it is necessary to examine whether other factors during those years influenced the outcome.

sections.title: Coincidence vs Common Cause
sections.content: Two major global events may occur at the same time, but that does not necessarily mean they are related. If the events occur due to separate reasons, it may simply be coincidence. On the other hand, if both events are influenced by the same global pressure or economic crisis, then there may be a common cause. Questions often require identifying that simultaneous timing does not automatically imply causation.

sections.title: Feedback Loops
sections.content: In a feedback loop, cause and effect continuously influence each other. For example, if inflation rises, workers demand higher wages. Higher wages increase production costs, which may further increase inflation. In such situations, it becomes difficult to identify the original cause and the resulting reaction.

sections.title: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc Fallacy
sections.content: This is a common logical error meaning that if event B occurs after event A, people assume that A caused B. At Level 3, avoiding this fallacy is extremely important. Assuming causation purely based on sequence can lead to incorrect conclusions.

sections.title: Deep Evaluation of Scope and Magnitude
sections.content: At Level 3, the scale and impact of both cause and effect are very important. If a small local factor is used to explain a large global outcome, the reasoning may be weak. Similarly, if the result is extremely large, it may actually be the result of multiple combined causes.

sections.title: Types of Questions Asked in Exams
sections.content: 1. Whether statement I can realistically be the long-term cause of statement II. 2. Whether the two events occurred together merely by coincidence. 3. Whether both events arise from a hidden larger cause. 4. Whether the statements represent a feedback loop situation.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Treating time sequence as proof of causation. 2. Ignoring the possibility of multiple factors behind global events. 3. Failing to separate the original cause from the reaction in feedback loops. 4. Confusing coincidence with common cause.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: At Level 3, analyzing cause and effect requires understanding time delays, global influences, and feedback cycles. Avoid the post hoc fallacy and always verify whether a real logical relationship exists.

tricks.title: Post Hoc Fallacy Check
tricks.explanation: If event B happens after event A, do not immediately assume A caused B. First consider other possible causes.
tricks.example: A policy was implemented and later the economy grew. It does not necessarily mean that policy caused the growth.

tricks.title: Time Lag Analysis
tricks.explanation: If the result appears years later, consider the intermediate events as well.
tricks.example: A country changed its trade policy and exports increased years later. Other economic reforms may also have contributed.

tricks.title: Coincidence Detection
tricks.explanation: Two major events can occur at the same time but may simply be coincidence.
tricks.example: Two countries experienced economic decline in the same year but due to different reasons.

tricks.title: Common Cause Search
tricks.explanation: If multiple events occur globally, check whether a shared pressure or crisis exists.
tricks.example: Economic decline across several countries may be caused by a global recession.

tricks.title: Feedback Loop Identification
tricks.explanation: If the effect again influences the original cause, a feedback loop may exist.
tricks.example: Inflation rises → wages increase → production costs increase → inflation rises again.

tricks.title: Magnitude Consistency Rule
tricks.explanation: If the result is very large, the cause should also be large or involve multiple factors.
tricks.example: A small policy change cannot transform the entire global economy.

tricks.title: Hidden Variable Trick
tricks.explanation: If the connection between two events is unclear, consider the possibility of a hidden third factor.
tricks.example: Demand for two industries suddenly increases. Economic growth might be the hidden cause.

tricks.title: Cause vs Reaction Check
tricks.explanation: Sometimes an event is actually a reaction rather than the original cause.
tricks.example: Companies raised prices because production costs had already increased.

tricks.title: Systemic Pressure Rule
tricks.explanation: If multiple countries or institutions are affected simultaneously, it may be due to a larger systemic pressure.
tricks.example: Several currencies weakened due to a global financial crisis.

tricks.title: Logical Sequence Mapping
tricks.explanation: Map the full chain of events to identify where the real cause began.
tricks.example: Energy prices rise → production costs increase → product prices increase → inflation rises.
